Marl Sedge's report: through the night and morning she counted a skiff with four men (one lean, in brown) put in at the boat-shed at dawn; two more with pikes walked in along the far shore road; a tall hooded man in grey arrived by a closed carriage at mid-morning and went into the shed. You ride up beside the wagon and murmur your warning. Corvin inclines his head. "Not a syllable, my dear, that isn't in the plan." Pell grunts. You give the order and the column moves out, six guards in grey behind the wagon, Kit at your shoulder, and you hum the road song low until the guards stop fidgeting with their crossbows. Your Perception check on the road is a 21. Nothing follows you. The road behind is empty to the horizon.

You reach the landward end of the Gannet Causeway at half past noon. The flats are a wide bright mud, the channel is still running, and the causeway is a dark wet line across it, not yet fully clear. Marl Sedge slides out of the reeds beside the road as if she had grown there, her cloak crusted with salt.

She gives her count in a flat whisper. At dawn a skiff put in at the boat-shed with four men, one of them lean, in a brown coat. Two more with pikes came along the far shore road on foot. At mid-morning a closed carriage arrived, and a tall hooded man in grey stepped out and went into the shed. Seven or eight in all, she says. And the reeds you laid across the mooring-stake's path are crossed.

They are waiting for the water to drop. The causeway opens around two o'clock, with an hour and a half to wait. The six guards can go into the landward reeds now, quietly. The wagon can wait at the causeway's mouth in plain sight, as bait should. Corvin sits on the bench with his eyes closed, and his lips are moving. You can't tell whether he is praying or counting.

You have all three slots, all three Inspirations, 17 hit points, and Kit. What does Wren do?

sheet.name: Wren Ashgrove
sheet.opening: Wren Ashgrove, a half-elf bard of about nineteen with a quick grin and a sharper tongue, arrives at dusk in the river-market town of Marrowford, a few weeks after fleeing the caravan of her mentor Corvin Tallowmere. She was raised by him as a storyteller's apprentice, and she left in the night at a river crossing with his ledger of forged tales sold to nobles (its pages now hidden in the binding of her road-psalter), a few of his best forgeries, and a head start. She carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, a gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers whom Corvin worshipped only as cover; it holds a curl of yellowed parchment in an unknown hand that may be a true blessing or another forgery. She does not know if Corvin has sent anyone after her. Her ideal: stories should be free, and truth is whatever people can be made to believe. Her bond: find the nobles Corvin cheated and decide whether to expose him or quietly fix what he did. Her flaw: she can't resist a secret, and she lies even when the truth would serve her better. She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. The hook: as she reaches the market square, she spots a caravan wagon with Corvin's painted shrine-lantern sigil parked at the edge of town, but no sign of Corvin. A frightened young page in a minor noble's livery is pressing a sealed letter into the hands of the wagon's driver, and the seal looks like one Wren has seen in the ledger. Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. You ride up beside the wagon and murmur your warning. Corvin inclines his head. "Not a word that isn't in the plan, child. Though it is a poor plan with no words in it." Pell, riding on the far side, shifts his halberd meaningfully, and Corvin falls silent with great dignity.

Near midnight a skiff with two men slid into the boat-shed creek, one lean and in a brown coat. They cut reeds and hid the skiff, and one went off on foot to the north. The ebb will uncover the causeway about two. The guards can slip into the landward reeds before then, out of sight of the far bank, and you have more than two hours to settle how this goes. You have three slots, three Inspirations, Kit, Pell, and a lure in your saddlebag. What does Wren do?

entries.text: notebook: updated Marl Sedge

You lean from Ember toward the wagon and tell Corvin that one stray word will earn him Pell's gag. He lifts his shackled hands in mock surrender. "I'll be a mouse," he says. Then you give the order and lead the column out, humming the road song low. By the third verse two of the guards are humming with you, which steadies them.

It's a slow ride over the dike roads, and the sun is high when the flats open ahead, bright and flat, with the causeway still half under water. It is about half past eleven. The ebb has begun, and the road will clear in a couple of hours. Your Perception on arrival is a 9, and you notice nothing wrong at the landward end.

Marl finds you before you find her. She rises out of the reeds like a heron and walks beside Ember's stirrup.

"Two men, in the dark, at the turn of the tide," she murmurs. "A skiff with no light. One lean, with a walk like a man testing ice. One broad. They stayed an hour at the boat-shed, put a cask and a coil of rope under the floor, and went off upriver. I climb down off the table, thank the drover with a coin, and take Kit and Pell aside. "Sparrow's ahead of us and headed for Osric. I want to ride at first light with Kit and two fast guards on the best horses, hard enough to reach Thornhallow by midday and warn Lord Edric and Osric. I order a bed for the night, check my slots and Ember's feed, and write a short note to Lord Edric to send ahead by the swiftest rider tonight: "Sparrow comes to Osric, bar the chapel and keep him inside the manor. W."

You press a coin into the drover's hand and draw Kit and Pell into the corner by the hearth. Pell hears you out with his jaw working. "Two of my best on the fast horses, then. I don't like splitting the guard with Harrow's people about, but I like a dead chaplain less." He agrees to bring the wagon behind at its own pace, and Tam Rudd rides in it with the prisoners. Kit only says, "Hard riding, then," and goes to see to her saddle.

You pay for a bed with two silver, check Ember's feed and hooves, and write your note by a stub of candle: "Sparrow comes to Osric, bar the chapel and keep him inside the manor. W." The landlord's son has the fastest cob in the yard. He takes the letter and a silver coin and rides into the dark toward Thornhallow, with the lantern bobbing until the road swallows it.

You sleep four hours, wake at the first grey, and ride at six with Kit and two grey-cloaked guards, Dunmore and Aye-Hal, on the best horses. The road is firm and dry. You hold a canter and walk the horses to breathe, and the river glints to your left. The miles go by in rooks and stubble.

Near the last bend before Thornhallow you are watching the hedgerows so hard that you miss the hedgerows. Your Perception is a 5, and you see nothing but green. Kit doesn't speak, but she does touch her sword.

It is about midday on Day 18 when the grey walls and the green and white pennant of Thornhallow rise over the field. The gatehouse is open. Smoke rises from the village, and the chapel bell is silent. You have 17 of 17 hit points, three slots, three Inspirations and 71 gp, 1 sp and 4 cp. What does Wren do?

You thank the drover with a coin and take Kit and Pell aside in the stable yard. Pell scratches his jaw. "Splitting a column is how you lose one," he says. But he gives way, with a condition: the wagon keeps six guards and he stays with it, and the two fastest riders go with you. Tam Rudd rides with Pell. "If that brown coat is ahead of you, better a warned lord than a tidy column."

You write the note by the tap-room lamp and seal it with plain wax: "Sparrow comes to Osric. Bar the chapel and keep him inside the manor. W." The landlord's son has the best horse in the yard. He takes it into the dark for the price of a silver penny, and you hear the hooves fade up the river road.

You sleep a short night in a narrow bed, with the lamp-staff against the wall and Kit across the door. Ember is fed and rubbed down. You wake in the dark, and the four of you leave at first light with a second pair of guards, Dunstan and a quiet young woman called Ferrel. You ride hard along the river road, walking the horses in the shallows and trotting on the flat. The mist burns off by mid-morning, the hedgerows go by, and the river keeps pace on your left.

At about noon the grey wall of Thornhallow comes up around the bend, with its green and white pennant over the gatehouse and the smoke of the village behind. The gate is shut. A guard in Verrel green stands on the wall-walk and looks down at four riders in Vantry grey and one in a road-stained coat. The chapel roof is visible above the wall, and a thin line of smoke rises from the green chapel's chimney. You have 17 of 17 hit points, three slots and three Inspirations. The rest of the column is half a day behind you. What does Wren do?

sheet.name: Wren Ashgrove
sheet.opening: Wren Ashgrove, a half-elf bard of about nineteen with a quick grin and a sharper tongue, arrives at dusk in the river-market town of Marrowford, a few weeks after fleeing the caravan of her mentor Corvin Tallowmere. She was raised by him as a storyteller's apprentice, and she left in the night at a river crossing with his ledger of forged tales sold to nobles (its pages now hidden in the binding of her road-psalter), a few of his best forgeries, and a head start. She carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, a gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers whom Corvin worshipped only as cover; it holds a curl of yellowed parchment in an unknown hand that may be a true blessing or another forgery. She does not know if Corvin has sent anyone after her. Her ideal: stories should be free, and truth is whatever people can be made to believe. Her bond: find the nobles Corvin cheated and decide whether to expose him or quietly fix what he did. Her flaw: she can't resist a secret, and she lies even when the truth would serve her better. She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. The hook: as she reaches the market square, she spots a caravan wagon with Corvin's painted shrine-lantern sigil parked at the edge of town, but no sign of Corvin. A frightened young page in a minor noble's livery is pressing a sealed letter into the hands of the wagon's driver, and the seal looks like one Wren has seen in the ledger. Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. Open on Wren in the square, with the choice of how to approach the wagon and the page, and a locked iron-bound strongbox on the wagon's tailboard that she itches to poke at.

input.add_to_description: Day 17 night: Wren sent a rider ahead to Thornhallow with a note to Lord Edric ("Sparrow comes to Osric, bar the chapel and keep him inside the manor. W."). At first light Day 18 Wren, Kit and two guards on the best horses ride hard for Thornhallow; Pell follows with the wagon and prisoners at a safer pace.

entries.text: notebook: updated Sparrow

You climb down from the table, press a coin into the drover's palm, and draw Kit and Pell into the corner by the hearth. Pell hears you out with his jaw working. "Splitting the column with Sparrow loose," he says. "I don't like it. But I like a priest with a knife in him less." He picks the two guards himself, a lean pair named Dunstan and Wick who ride better than they march, and says he'll keep the wagon tight, with Marl Sedge's old habits and the whole watch doubled.

You pay for a bed, and the landlord's wife shows you to a cot over the kitchen. Before you sleep you write the note on the back of a tavern bill, small and plain: "Sparrow comes to Osric. Bar the chapel and keep him inside the manor. W." You seal it with a dab of wax and your thumb. A stable lad called Harl takes it on the best horse the inn has, a rangy bay, and clatters out into the dark. You check Ember's feed and your slots, and you're asleep in minutes.

Kit wakes you at twenty past five, and the sky in the east is the colour of a pewter plate. You're at 17 of 17, with all three slots and three Inspirations. The horses are saddled in the yard with their breath smoking. Dunstan and Wick wait by their mounts with spare water. Pell stands at the wagon's tail, and across the yard Corvin and Ansel are being loaded, blinking and silent. Corvin catches your eye. "Mind the priest, child," he says dryly. "Sparrow doesn't forget a wound."

Thornhallow is a hard morning's ride away, and the road runs flat along the river. What does Wren do?

input.add_to_description: Day 17 night: Wren sent a rider ahead with a note to Lord Edric ("Sparrow comes to Osric, bar the chapel and keep him inside the manor. W."). Day 18 dawn at Thornhallow: Edric's men turned away a lean stranger in a brown coat, arm stiff, who asked for Osric at the chapel door; he left toward the mill lane. Wren, Kit and two guards ride ahead at first light; Pell follows with the wagon and prisoners (Ansel, Corvin, Tam Rudd).

entries.text: notebook: updated Sparrow

You tip the drover and take Kit and Pell aside. Pell grumbles about splitting his column, but he agrees. He gives you two of his best riders, Dunn and Aske, and promises to bring the wagon, the prisoners and the rest of the guard at a steady pace behind you. You write your note to Lord Edric by candle: "Sparrow comes to Osric, bar the chapel and keep him inside the manor. W." A guard with the swiftest horse takes it into the dark. You pay for a bed, check your slots and see to Ember's feed.

At first light the four of you ride hard. The road is dry, and you keep the horses at a trot and a canter by turns. The river glints on your left, and you pass the ruined mill and the miller's cottage at Dunnock Ford without stopping. Aske says the rider will have reached Thornhallow before dawn.

At noon you come over the last rise, and Thornhallow sits in its river bend with the green and white pennant over the gatehouse. A guard in Verrel green is waiting in the road. He salutes and says Lord Edric got your note before sunrise. At dawn, he adds, a lean stranger in a brown coat, with one arm held stiff, came to the chapel door asking for Brother Osric. The men Lord Edric had set there turned him away, and he left up the mill lane without a fuss. Nobody has seen him since. Osric is inside the manor, grumbling about his psalter. Lord Edric is waiting for you in the hall.

It's noon on Day 18. You have 17 of 17 hit points, three slots and three Inspirations. Pell's wagon with Ansel and Corvin is half a day behind, and Sparrow is loose somewhere near the village. What does Wren do?

input.add_to_description: Day 18 dusk, Thornhallow study (Wren's Insight 13, one short of 14): told Lord Edric to his face, with Osric, Wren, Kit and guards present, that he is the son of Hugh Verrel, Aldous's eldest, who did not drown at nineteen but was cast out for marrying Joan, a tenant's daughter, and died of a winter fever in Marrowford when Ansel was six; Aldous had the baptism scraped. Ansel grew up a clerk's boy and then a patron of road-shrines. Edric heard him in silence. Wren could not tell whether he left anything out; he skipped lightly past how he came to take the name of the dead child Aldous the younger. Corvin waits in the gatehouse under watch; Hale is still in the cellar.

entries.text: notebook: updated Ansel Verrel

In the yard you tell Pell quietly that Ansel goes up first with two guards, and Corvin waits in the gatehouse until you send for him. Pell nods and doesn't argue. Corvin watches Ansel's chains pass and says nothing.

You walk Ansel up to Lord Edric's door yourself. "He's ready to tell it his own way, my lord. Ansel, say it plain, and let Osric hear every word." Then you take your place inside the door with your back to the wall, one hand on the lamp-staff and Kit beside you. The study is lit by two candles. Osric sits with the register open on his knees.

Ansel stands, because the chains won't let him sit comfortably. He looks at Edric a long moment, at the chin they share.

"Hugh Verrel was my father," he says. "He didn't drown. He married a tenant's daughter named Joan, and Aldous cast him out and had the baptism scraped. My father died of a winter fever in Marrowford when I was six. I grew up a clerk's boy, and later I paid for road-shrines because a priest's lamp was the only light that ever shone on me. I'm not here for Thornhallow, cousin. I'm here because you should hear it from the one who has most to answer for."

Edric says nothing. His hand creeps toward the register and stops. Osric, very quietly, says, "The ink matches the scrape, my lord. I believe him."

Your Insight is a 13, one short of what you needed. His grief sounds true, and Hugh and Joan sound true. But when he speaks of how he came to take a dead child's name, he moves past it lightly, and you can't tell whether that's shame or something kept back.

It's ten to seven on Day 18. Edric is staring at the cousin he was told never lived. Corvin is in the gatehouse, Hale is in the cellar, and Sparrow sleeps under guard. You have 17 of 17 hit points, three slots and three Inspirations. What does Wren do?

Corvin gives you a look of mild interest as they lead him off, like a man watching a play he has already read.

It stopped when your father died." His voice stays level. "Brother, the scraped line in your book is mine."

Osric closes his eyes. Edric makes a sound like a man stepping onto ice that cracks. "You took a child's grave for a name," he says. "Why?" Ansel almost smiles. Crowe will ask it better." You can't tell whether that's honour or a door he's keeping shut.

Edric sits down slowly. No one speaks. The candles burn, and below in the gatehouse Corvin is waiting for his turn.

input.add_to_description: Day 20: Wren, Kit and a watchman rode the east road after the hand-cart rut. Survival 7 and Persuasion 8 both failed: the rut was lost among market-day carts at the first crossroads, and the toll-keepers were hostile and vague. The trail is cold. entries.text: notebook: updated Dunstan Crake
time: 6 hours later: Day 20, 3:20:06 PM

Lyle agrees to hold the chest, and the bridge-house stable lends you two fast horses. You, Kit and a young watchman named Pip ride out the east gate with her promise in your ears: the clerk opens it at noon in front of her and a notary.

The trail does not cooperate. Your Survival is a 7. The cart rut runs a quarter-mile along the east road, then joins the crossroads at Tanner's Cross, where it is lost under a market-day tangle of grain wagons, drovers' hooves and a dozen other hand-carts. You walk the verge for half an hour and cannot say which line is the one you want.

The gate-keepers are no better. Your Persuasion is an 8. The toll-keeper at the crossroads says he sees "grey coats by the dozen, mistress, and ears by the pair," and the miller's wife at the next bridge-house shuts her shutter on you. Pip mutters that east-road folk don't love bridge-house badges. Kit sits her horse like a post and says, "Cold."

You ride a wide loop back by the river path in case the cart went to a landing, and find only reeds and one fisherman who has seen nothing. You return to the Marrowford gate at twenty past three, tired and empty-handed.

Warden Lyle meets you at the bridge-house with her keys. The clerk came at noon, and the chest was opened before her and a notary. It held ten years of grain accounts, dull and honest-looking, with not a name in them you didn't already know. Oake sits in his cell and says nothing.

You borrow two fast horses from the bridge-house stable and tell Lyle, "If the clerk arrives at noon, he opens the chest in front of you and a notary. I'll be back by dusk." She grunts and promises the seal will stay whole.

Then it goes badly. The east road is the busiest in Marrowford, and by mid-morning a dozen carts have crossed the rut you were following. Your Survival is a 4. The depth tells you nothing, and the fresh track blurs into the old. At the east gate you try the keeper with a brisk, clever manner, and your Persuasion is a natural 1. He takes it for mockery and answers every question with "Can't say, mistress." The watchman has to wheedle a grudging "a cart, maybe, before dawn" out of him. At a crossroads four miles out the ruts fork three ways, toward the upper ford, the hills and the old Ashby road. You and Kit spend the day riding each branch for a mile. You find a farmer who saw "a lean fellow" go by, and a ditch with a broken cart-wheel, and nothing that ties to Oake.

You turn back with tired horses. It is twenty past five on Day 20 when the bridge-house comes in sight. Lyle meets you at the door. Dame Crowe's clerk came at noon, she says, and the chest was opened before her and a notary. It held only grain accounts, dull and honest, and he left unimpressed. Oake, hearing, merely smiled. Pell's wagon with Corvin is due at the gates tonight.

You have 17 of 17 hit points, three slots and three Inspirations, and 78 gp. Crake, Sedley and the real papers are gone, and the assize is ten days off. What does Wren do?

sheet.name: Wren Ashgrove
sheet.opening: Wren Ashgrove, a half-elf bard of about nineteen with a quick grin and a sharper tongue, arrives at dusk in the river-market town of Marrowford, a few weeks after fleeing the caravan of her mentor Corvin Tallowmere. She was raised by him as a storyteller's apprentice, and she left in the night at a river crossing with his ledger of forged tales sold to nobles (its pages now hidden in the binding of her road-psalter), a few of his best forgeries, and a head start. She carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, a gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers whom Corvin worshipped only as cover; it holds a curl of yellowed parchment in an unknown hand that may be a true blessing or another forgery. She does not know if Corvin has sent anyone after her. Her ideal: stories should be free, and truth is whatever people can be made to believe. Her bond: find the nobles Corvin cheated and decide whether to expose him or quietly fix what he did. Her flaw: she can't resist a secret, and she lies even when the truth would serve her better. She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. The hook: as she reaches the market square, she spots a caravan wagon with Corvin's painted shrine-lantern sigil parked at the edge of town, but no sign of Corvin. A frightened young page in a minor noble's livery is pressing a sealed letter into the hands of the wagon's driver, and the seal looks like one Wren has seen in the ledger. Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. Open on Wren in the square, with the choice of how to approach the wagon and the page, and a locked iron-bound strongbox on the wagon's tailboard that she itches to poke at.

You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

time: 4 hours later: Day 20, 1:20:06 PM

You borrow two fast horses from the bridge-house stable, and Lyle agrees: if the clerk comes at noon, the chest is opened before her and a notary, and you will be back by dusk. Kit and a young watchman named Piers ride out with you by the east gate.

The rut is easy to find and hard to read. Your Survival is a 12. It tells you the cart was heavy and a day old, but at a crossing of the tracks the marks tangle into a mess of wheels. The gatekeepers are kinder. Your Persuasion is a 20. The east-gate sentry remembers a grey-coated man with a notched ear and a thin, frightened clerk pushing a laden hand-cart out at dusk the day before. They paid a carter at Fallow Cross, two miles out, to take the load north on the Ashby road. The carter, a woman at the crossing's alehouse, confirms it. She says they were in a hurry and paid in silver.

North means the Ashby road, with Lantern's Rest half a day up it and Ashby Weir beyond. A day-old head start on a carter's wagon can't be closed by evening, and you promised Lyle you'd be back. You turn the horses at Fallow Cross and ride in under the bridge-house arch at twenty past one, with the noon hour missed and the clerk's visit still ahead of you.

You have 17 of 17 hit points, three slots and three Inspirations, and 78 gp. The chest is still under seal, Dame Crowe's clerk is expected soon, and Pell's wagon will be at the gates by dusk. Crake and Sedley carry Oake's real papers north. What does Wren do?
